issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames the study as using a national probability/general population/nationally representative sample, but the Methods state that participants were recruited from an introductory psychology participant pool and were young, mostly female students. This is a fundamental contradiction that affects interpretation, external validity, and the paper’s central rationale contrasting student versus general-population samples.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington. This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The Discussion and Conclusion claim national representativeness and high generalisability, but the reported sample is a small introductory psychology pool from one university, predominantly Pākehā, female, and age 19. These characteristics do not support inference to the New Zealand population and directly undermine the paper’s claim that it advances prior student-sample research by using a general population sample.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistency with table statistics
issues.description: The Methods report N = 374, but Table 1 correlations have extremely narrow confidence intervals that are inconsistent with a sample of 374. For example, r = .21 with a 95% CI of [.18, .23] would require a much larger sample. This suggests either the sample size, table, or analytic description is wrong, preventing evaluation of precision and statistical power.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study...

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistency with table confidence intervals
issues.description: The confidence intervals around means and standard deviations are implausibly narrow for N = 374. For example, an SD of 1.40 and N = 374 would yield a standard error around .07 and a 95% CI for the mean roughly ±.14, not ±.03–.04. This indicates either a much larger N was used, the reported N is wrong, or confidence intervals were incorrectly calculated/reported.

The environmental outcome is described inconsistently as willingness to change behavior, willingness to sacrifice, and concern about environmental problems. These are distinct constructs. The inconsistency makes it unclear what was actually analyzed and whether the conclusions match the measure.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and analyses frame the outcome as environmentalism or willingness to change/sacrifice behavior, but the Methods describe only two items assessing concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. Concern and perceived exaggeration are not equivalent to behavioral willingness or sacrifice, and neither directly measures actual pro-environmental behavior. This threatens construct validity and the interpretation of the cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: The Data Analysis section states that the path analysis examined willingness to sacrifice, but the preceding Measures section says the environmentalism measure assessed concern about environmental problems. The discrepancy suggests either the wrong measure is described, the wrong variable label is used, or the Results interpret a different construct than measured.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: Table 1 labels WILL as willingness to make sacrifices for the environment, whereas the Measures section lists items about environmental concern and exaggeration. The table label therefore appears inconsistent with the operational definition, making the reported descriptive statistics and correlations difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Note. SDO = social dominance orientation, RWA = right-wing authoritarianism, WILL = willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.description: Environmentalism is represented by only two items, one positively worded concern item and one reverse-coded perceived exaggeration item. A two-item measure is vulnerable to low content validity, wording/method effects, and ambiguity about whether it captures concern, skepticism, or willingness to sacrifice. No justification is provided for treating these items as a broad environmentalism construct across five years.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants’ concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley’s [28] environmental concern scale, “How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?” and “To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?”.

issues.description: The study compares constructs longitudinally across five waves and estimates cross-lagged paths, but does not report tests of longitudinal measurement invariance for SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. Without evidence that the scales measure the same constructs over time, apparent stability and cross-lagged change may reflect changes in measurement properties rather than substantive change.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: One RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but included at other time points. This creates non-equivalent measurement across waves, threatens longitudinal comparability, and is especially problematic in a cross-lagged model if measurement invariance and handling of the missing item are not clearly described.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The manuscript does not explain how the missing RWA item at Time 2 was handled in scale scoring or latent measurement. If listwise deletion was used at the item level, all participants would be missing that item at Time 2; if the scale was scored with five items at Time 2 and six at other waves, the construct metric differs over time. This omission prevents replication and evaluation of longitudinal validity.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: Analyses used listwise deletion in a five-wave longitudinal study. Listwise deletion is generally inefficient and can bias estimates unless data are missing completely at random, an assumption not assessed or reported. Modern approaches such as FIML or multiple imputation would usually be preferable, especially for panel data with attrition.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report initial sample size, retention at each wave, attrition rates, or whether attrition was selective by demographics or key variables. Because listwise deletion was used, the final analytic sample may be a biased subset of those originally recruited, affecting internal validity and generalizability.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013). Of the 374 participants included in this study... Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The manuscript refers readers to a website for full procedural, retention, and demographic details rather than reporting essential information in the article. Key details needed to evaluate recruitment, follow-up, timing, incentives, consent, and attrition are missing from the manuscript itself, limiting reproducibility and peer review.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The title, abstract, and current study describe a five-year longitudinal analysis, but the Methods state participants were recruited across five semesters. Five semesters is approximately 2.5 years, not five years, unless the semesters were annual measurement occasions. The timing and lag length are therefore unclear and potentially misrepresented.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The manuscript does not specify exact time intervals between measurement occasions, despite using lagged effects and stationarity assumptions. Cross-lagged effects depend on lag length; unclear timing prevents interpretation of effect size and replication.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).

issues.description: The Data Analysis section redundantly states twice that cross-lagged associations were constrained to equality, suggesting either a drafting error or confusion about what constraints were imposed. It is unclear whether autoregressive paths, residual covariances, factor loadings, intercepts, or only cross-lagged paths were constrained.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point. We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: The manuscript calls the analysis path analysis but then discusses item residual variances, implying a latent variable SEM. It does not report whether constructs were modeled as latent factors or observed scale scores, whether factor loadings/intercepts were constrained, whether residual covariances were allowed, or whether within-wave covariances were estimated. These details are essential to evaluate a cross-lagged panel model.
issues.quote: We used path analysis to examine associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.description: The reported RMSEA point estimate is outside its confidence interval: RMSEA = .03 but 90% CI [.025, .026]. A point estimate cannot fall outside its confidence interval, indicating a reporting or calculation error.

The model has very poor chi-square and suboptimal CFI (.86), but the manuscript accepts the model based on RMSEA and SRMR. A CFI of .86 is generally below conventional thresholds, and the enormous chi-square relative to df suggests substantial misfit. Accepting the model without discussing implications or alternative specifications weakens confidence in the estimated paths.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: Several nested model comparisons omit the chi-square symbol and report values as '2(1)', which is ambiguous and appears to be a formatting/statistical reporting error. Proper reporting should state Δχ²(df) and include the estimation method and correction if robust estimators were used.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126

issues.subcategory: incorrect conclusion from nested model comparison
issues.description: The authors claim SDO is a stronger predictor than RWA despite a nested model comparison showing that constraining the paths equal did not significantly worsen fit. This directly undermines the claim of a statistically stronger SDO effect; interpreting SDO as stronger based only on coefficient pattern is not warranted as an inferential claim.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data 2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The Discussion states that SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA, but the Results report a non-significant model comparison for the equality of those paths. This is a direct contradiction and overstates the statistical evidence.
issues.quote: In this context, both SDO and RWA are related to environmentalism, but SDO is a significantly stronger prospective predictor than RWA.

issues.description: The reported difference test comparing RWA-to-SDO and SDO-to-RWA paths is extraordinarily large (15,389.13) for a one-degree-of-freedom test, especially given the small reported coefficients (.02 vs -.001) and the reported sample of 374. This is likely a typographical, scaling, or model comparison error that requires correction.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.description: Regression/path coefficients are reported with 'SD' instead of the conventional 'SE'. If these are standard errors, the label is wrong; if they are standard deviations, the inferential statistics are unclear. This affects interpretability and reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01]).

issues.description: The Data Analysis section says standardized parameters are presented, while Figure 1 and Results report unstandardized parameters. This inconsistency matters because standardized and unstandardized coefficients answer different comparative questions, especially when comparing predictors with different variances.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances.

issues.description: The figure caption says unstandardized parameters are shown, contradicting the Methods statement that standardized parameters are presented. It is unclear which estimates underlie the conclusions.
issues.quote: Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The Methods state that p < .05 was adopted, whereas the Figure caption says all paths meet p < .01 unless otherwise noted. The abstract and results also emphasize significance without a consistent threshold. This inconsistency can create ambiguity about which effects are considered statistically reliable.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.subcategory: large sample claim inconsistent with reported N
issues.description: The authors justify a significance threshold by referring to the large sample size, but the Methods report only 374 participants. For a five-wave SEM with many parameters and listwise deletion, N = 374 is not especially large and may be marginal depending on model complexity.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: If the analytic sample is truly 374, fitting a five-wave model with three constructs, multiple items, constrained residuals, and many lagged paths may be underpowered or unstable, particularly for small cross-lagged effects. No power analysis, simulation, or parameter-to-sample justification is provided.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study... The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus

issues.subcategory: causal claims from observational cross-lagged data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly makes causal claims from observational survey data. Cross-lagged panel models can establish temporal ordering under assumptions, but they do not rule out unmeasured confounding, stable between-person differences, common-method effects, or time-varying confounders. The claim that ideology causes environmentalism is therefore too strong.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.description: The abstract and discussion infer that the motivation to exploit the environment comes from dominance and submission to authority. The measures did not assess motivation to exploit the environment or mechanisms, only self-reported ideological attitudes and environmental concern/willingness. This is an overinterpretation of correlational longitudinal associations.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.

issues.description: The model does not appear to adjust for plausible confounders such as political ideology/party identification, socioeconomic status, education, religiosity, personality, cohort, gender, or baseline environmental experiences. These variables could influence both SDO/RWA and environmental attitudes, biasing cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The traditional cross-lagged panel model conflates within-person change with stable between-person differences unless random intercepts or comparable methods are used. The manuscript interprets cross-lagged coefficients as within-person change and influence, but does not separate within- and between-person effects.
issues.quote: These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships, and suggest that SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse.

issues.description: The claim that analyses 'disentangle directionality' is too strong because reciprocal cross-lagged associations in observational data do not establish causal direction absent stronger assumptions and controls. Temporal precedence alone is insufficient.
issues.quote: These analyses help us disentangle the directionality of the relationships

issues.description: A key theoretical rationale is that the study extends prior student-sample longitudinal work by using a general population sample. The Methods instead describe a student participant pool. This undermines the conceptual contribution and the interpretation that differences from prior work are due to sample type.
issues.quote: We expand on Stanley et al.’s study by using a large, national probability sample spanning five years to examine how these variables relate over time in the general population.

issues.description: The manuscript infers from lagged associations between RWA and SDO that New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism more than social dominance. This macro-socialization claim is not measured and cannot be inferred from the reported individual-level cross-lagged coefficients, especially from a student sample.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: The Introduction notes that RWA dimensions may differentially predict environmental attitudes, but the study uses a short six-item RWA scale and treats RWA as unidimensional. Without reporting item content, dimensional coverage, or factor structure, it is unclear whether the measure captures submission, aggression, and conventionalism sufficiently to support claims about tradition and authority.
issues.quote: Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items from Altemeyer’s [27] RWA scale.

issues.description: The manuscript discusses dominance versus anti-egalitarianism and competing mechanisms, but uses a short SDO6 total score without distinguishing dimensions. This limits the ability to draw conclusions about whether effects reflect desire for dominance, anti-egalitarianism, or other components.
issues.quote: Social dominance orientation was assessed using six items from Sidanius and Pratto’s [1] SDO6 scale. Three items favoured dominance... and three favoured equality...

issues.description: The manuscript does not state how reverse-coded items were handled, whether scale scores were averaged or summed, how many valid item responses were required, or whether higher scores consistently represent higher SDO/RWA/environmentalism. These details are needed to replicate the analysis and interpret coefficients.
issues.quote: Participants rated the extent to which they agreed with each item on 7-point Likert scales, from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.description: Only Time 1 reliabilities appear in Table 1, and the manuscript does not report reliability across all five waves or for the environmentalism measure at each wave. Longitudinal reliability is important because measurement error can attenuate stability and cross-lagged paths.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1. Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used...

issues.description: SDO and RWA reliabilities of .69 and .70 are modest, and environmentalism appears to be only .76 with two items. Measurement error may bias cross-lagged estimates and comparisons of predictor strength, particularly if reliability differs across constructs or waves. The authors acknowledge poorer reliabilities but do not address implications analytically.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.description: Only Time 1 descriptive statistics and correlations are reported. For a five-wave longitudinal study, means, standard deviations, reliabilities, and correlations across all waves are needed to evaluate stability, change, stationarity assumptions, attrition effects, and possible period effects.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.description: The manuscript does not mention preregistration, an a priori analysis plan, or whether hypotheses and model constraints were specified before data analysis. Given multiple possible model specifications, constructs, waves, missing-data approaches, and equality constraints, undisclosed analytic flexibility is a concern.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.subcategory: post hoc model acceptance and constraints
issues.description: The analysis imposes stationarity and other equality constraints because the authors were interested in overall effects, but does not report model comparisons supporting these constraints or whether alternative models were tested. This limits confidence that the chosen model was not selected post hoc.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.description: The manuscript says syntax will be available only upon acceptance. For peer review and replication assessment, model syntax should be available during review, especially given ambiguities in model specification and inconsistent reporting.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: All constructs were measured by self-report Likert scales in the same survey context, creating potential common method variance, consistency effects, and social desirability bias. The manuscript does not discuss or address this limitation.
issues.quote: Participants responded on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much), with a midpoint of 4 (somewhat).

issues.subcategory: climate change claims from general environmental items
issues.description: The Introduction and Discussion frequently interpret findings in terms of climate change mitigation and climate change attitudes, but the environmentalism items assess general state of the natural environment and exaggeration of environmental problems, not climate change specifically. General environmental concern may not map directly onto climate change denial, mitigation, or willingness to act on climate change.
issues.quote: While climate change is arguably the biggest environmental problem of our time...

issues.description: The sample is young, 68% female, and 86% Pākehā, but the manuscript does not acknowledge these limitations when generalizing. These demographics may influence ideological attitudes, environmental concern, and their longitudinal dynamics.
issues.quote: the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female. Furthermore, 76% of participants were born in New Zealand and the majority (86%) identified as Pākehā (New Zealand European).

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim about non-overlapping confidence intervals
issues.description: The manuscript states that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism is stronger than the RWA-environmentalism correlation based on non-overlapping confidence intervals. Non-overlap of separate CIs is not the proper test for comparing dependent correlations sharing a variable; a test for dependent correlations should be used.
issues.quote: Of note here is that the zero-order correlation between SDO and environmentalism was stronger than the correlation for RWA, as indicated by the non-overlapping confidence interval.

issues.description: The table note says confidence intervals are based on '1000 iterations' without specifying whether this refers to bootstrapping, Monte Carlo simulation, or another method, and without describing resampling units or handling of missingness. This is insufficient for replication and may be inappropriate if the data structure is longitudinal/panel.
issues.quote: Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.subcategory: nested comparison unclear under estimator and constraints
issues.description: The authors state that a traditional Wald test is impossible due to constraints and instead use model fit comparisons, but do not report whether the comparison used chi-square difference testing appropriate for the estimator, whether robust corrections were applied, or why Wald tests of equality constraints could not be conducted in Mplus. This makes the inference about path differences unreliable.
issues.quote: Due to the nature of the analysis and the constraints placed on the model, the traditional Wald test to confirm that SDO is a statistically stronger predictor than RWA is not possible. Instead, we imposed similar constraints on the model as in the Wald test...

issues.description: The model constrains cross-lagged effects to be time-invariant across five years, but does not report whether this stationarity assumption fits worse than a freely estimated model. If effects vary across waves, the pooled estimates may be misleading.
issues.quote: We tested the reciprocal influences between the constructs with a stationary cross-lagged model where all parameters are set as time-invariant.

issues.description: The authors constrain residual variances for the same item to equality over time but do not explain why, whether this was empirically supported, or whether other measurement parameters were constrained. Residual variance equality without establishing full measurement invariance may impose unjustified restrictions and contribute to poor model fit.
issues.quote: We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time, so item 1 in the SDO scale had equal residual variance across all time points.

issues.subcategory: missing estimator and treatment of ordinal data
issues.description: The measures use 7-point Likert items, but the manuscript does not report the Mplus estimator, whether items were treated as continuous or ordinal, whether robust standard errors were used, or how non-normality was handled. These choices affect fit indices, chi-square tests, and parameter estimates.
issues.quote: The model included three variables across five measurement points and was conducted in Mplus (version 7.3 [29]).

issues.description: No demographic or contextual covariates are included or discussed in the model despite reporting gender, age, birthplace, and ethnicity. The manuscript does not justify excluding these potential confounders or moderators.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study, the average age was 19 years at Time 1... and 68% were female.

issues.subcategory: accepted significance threshold contradiction with figure caption
issues.description: The figure caption states that all parameters meet p < .01 unless noted, while the Methods state p < .05 and the RWA effect is reported p = .001. The criteria for figure inclusion and interpretation are not consistently described.
issues.quote: All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The abstract says RWA was a significant negative predictor, but the comparative model did not support the claim that SDO is statistically stronger than RWA, and the measure of environmentalism is inconsistently described. The abstract simplifies and overstates inferential support.
issues.quote: RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor.

issues.subcategory: missing Figure 1 numerical details in text
issues.description: The manuscript refers to Figure 1 for autoregressive stability but does not provide the autoregressive coefficients, confidence intervals, or exact paths in the text. Because the figure is not fully reproduced in the manuscript excerpt and because standardized/unstandardized status is inconsistent, the main model estimates are incompletely reported.
issues.quote: As shown in Figure 1, across all time points, SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time

issues.description: The discussion elaborates environmental inequality, dominance over nature, dominance over social groups, and hierarchy enforcement mechanisms, but the study does not measure perceived hierarchy, environmental inequality, beneficiaries of exploitation, or dominance over nature. These mechanisms remain speculative and should not be presented as supported by the longitudinal analysis.
issues.quote: The preference for an unequal society leads individuals to be less willing to make personal sacrifices for the environment.

issues.description: The manuscript suggests high-SDO individuals should be targets for climate communications, but the study does not test communication interventions, message framing, or behavioral outcomes. This recommendation may be plausible but is not directly supported by the observational design.
issues.quote: Our findings highlight endorsers of SDO as targets for climate change communications.

issues.description: The Methods reference NZAVS details and acknowledge NZAVS data, but simultaneously say participants were recruited from the Victoria University introductory psychology pool. NZAVS is generally a national panel, while an introductory psychology pool is not. The source of data is unclear and internally contradictory.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report ethics approval, informed consent procedures, or participant protections. This is a reporting gap for human-subjects longitudinal research.
issues.quote: Participants and Procedure

issues.description: The Results claim variables were relatively stable over time but do not report the autoregressive coefficients or their confidence intervals. Without these, readers cannot evaluate stability, compare constructs, or assess whether stationarity constraints are plausible.
issues.quote: SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice were all relatively stable over time

issues.description: The manuscript states that 374 participants were included but does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria, whether participants needed complete data at all five waves, or whether exclusions occurred. This is especially important because listwise deletion was used.
issues.quote: Of the 374 participants included in this study

issues.description: Because only individuals included across the longitudinal analysis appear to be reported, the manuscript does not compare included versus excluded/dropout participants. If attrition relates to ideology or environmentalism, longitudinal associations may be biased.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.subcategory: confidence interval and p-value mismatch potential
issues.description: For RWA predicting environmentalism, the reported confidence interval [-.05, -.01] excludes zero and p = .001, but with B = -.02 and SD/SE = .01 this would imply a z around -2, not p = .001 unless the SE is smaller than rounded. Rounding may explain this, but the reporting is imprecise and should provide enough digits to verify the inference.

The authors compare the magnitude of SDO and RWA effects using unstandardized coefficients. Because SDO and RWA have different variances and possibly different reliabilities/scales, unstandardized coefficients do not directly indicate which construct is a stronger predictor in standardized terms. A standardized comparison or appropriate equality test is needed.
issues.quote: based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor

issues.subcategory: misalignment between environmental attitudes and exploitation
issues.description: The conclusion says desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism and the abstract says motivation to exploit the environment, but the outcome is concern/willingness rather than exploitation behavior or support for exploitation. Lower concern is not equivalent to active exploitation.
issues.quote: This result indicates that the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism in the future

issues.subcategory: wrong category label not permitted in manuscript interpretation
issues.description: The discussion treats environmentalism as a hierarchy-attenuating ideology based on theoretical reasoning, but the empirical outcome is an individual attitude item set. The term 'ideology' is not operationalized or tested and may overextend social dominance theory beyond the data.
issues.quote: Gaining similar opposition from Social Dominants, environmentalism is a hierarchy-attenuating ideology

issues.subcategory: missing item list for short scales
issues.description: Only example items are given for SDO and RWA. For short scales, exact item content matters because item selection can affect dimensional coverage, reliability, and longitudinal invariance. The full item list should be reported or provided in supplement.
issues.quote: These included items such as “Our country will be destroyed someday if we do not smash the perversions eating away at our moral fibre and traditional beliefs”.

issues.description: The diagonal of Table 1 lists .69, .70, and .76, apparently reliabilities, but the note does not explicitly say these are reliabilities or specify alpha/omega. This reduces clarity and reproducibility.

issues.subcategory: student sample not comparable to claimed general population literature
issues.description: The authors interpret differences from previous student-sample findings as reflecting the current study’s general population nature. Since the reported sample is also students, this comparison is invalid and the claimed contribution to population generalizability is unsupported.
issues.quote: It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.
